item.title: Astria vs FashionLab (2026): Which Is Better for Fashion Brands?
item.description: Astria vs FashionLab for fashion brands: a talent-marketplace content platform versus a production system for collections, categories, motion, and handoff.
item.content:encoded:
FashionLab has done something none of the other tools in this comparison have tried: it has put a talent marketplace next to the generator. Brands batch-produce on-model imagery through a five-step flow, and they can also hire AI creative directors, prompt engineers, retouchers, and 3D artists inside the same platform. Astria's answer to the same underlying problem is different—make the creative direction itself reusable, so the brand needs less external help each season.

The short answer: Astria is the clear overall winner for fashion brands producing a collection across its channels. Choose FashionLab if you want to hire AI creative talent and buy retouching alongside the tooling.

How we evaluated Astria and FashionLab​

We used six B2B buying questions: how the brand gets to a repeatable result, whether creative direction is owned or hired, casting and category depth, channel coverage, how the account structure and meter behave across a catalog, and what evidence supports each vendor.

Quick verdict: Astria vs FashionLab​

Decision factorFashionLabAstriaWinner

Professional fashion productionBatch on-model imagery from garment referencesBrand-directed production across ecommerce, lookbook, campaign, and socialAstria
Creative directionSelected per batch: model, pose, background, stylingApproved treatment — casting, styling, scene, crop, lighting, format — stored and reusedAstria
Casting and assetsFree AI model library, custom brand models, licensed digital twins, kids and size-inclusive castingModels across ages and body types, including children and extended-size casting, plus locations, poses, and brand referencesAstria

Access to AI creative talentMarketplace for creative directors, prompt engineers, retouchers, and 3D artistsNot offeredFashionLab
Best fitBrands wanting tooling plus hired creative talent in one placeFashion brands producing on-brand ecommerce, lookbook, campaign, and social assets across a collectionAstria
OverallA generator with a talent layer attachedThe stronger platform for professional fashion productionAstria

Reviewed September 1, 2026; no controlled image-quality benchmark was run.

FashionLab: generation plus a talent layer​

FashionLab positions itself for brand and marketing teams producing on-brand AI content, and its core flow is a clean five-step batch: select garment references as flat lay or on-body, assign models, choose pose, choose background, then generate dozens of looks with consistent models and backgrounds. Generation times are quoted around ninety seconds, and the company is unusually candid about disclosing the underlying generation model it uses.

Its casting options are broader than most small competitors: a free library of diverse AI models, custom brand-specific models, and the option to hire authorized digital twins of real models and influencers. Its published use cases include kids fashion—explicitly framed around avoiding the complexity of photoshoots with minors—and size inclusivity, both of which are real production needs that many tools in this category ignore. Credit where it is due: that is a thoughtful use-case set.

The genuinely novel part is the Creative Marketplace. Brands can hire specialized talent for creative direction, prompting, retouching, and project management; creators can find paid projects from brands. A separate in-built professional retouching service handles polished finishing at scale. No other product in this comparison bundles a labour market with the software.

The commercial structure needs care. The Basic plan is $20 a month and covers one brand and one project with two collaborator seats; extra seats are $20 a month each, four additional projects are $30 a month, and tokens are purchased separately at roughly $1.10–$1.20 each, with each generation consuming tokens according to resolution and complexity. Published proof is early: one named testimonial from a brand and marketing manager at Bruun Steengade, plus a reference to top Scandinavian brands.

Astria: a professional fashion-production environment​

Astria's answer to the same problem is to make outside expertise less necessary each season. Products, casting, references, templates, and outputs live in a brand workspace, and the approved treatment—casting, styling, scene, crop, lighting, format—is stored so the next person runs it rather than rebuilding it.

That extends across categories and channels. Templates cover beauty, jewelry, footwear, sports, luxury, and editorial as distinct disciplines; the casting library spans ages and body types, including children and extended-size casting, alongside locations, poses, and brand references; and campaign, editorial, social, and motion all derive from the same direction. When a brand does bring in an outside photographer or art director, that person works inside the workspace and leaves the treatment behind.

Public proof: an early reference base versus named brands​

FashionLab's public evidence is a single named testimonial and a regional claim. That is honest for a young product and it gives a buyer little to verify. Its marketplace, if it reaches liquidity, may become its strongest proof—brands returning to hire talent is a hard signal to fake.

Astria's public materials name fashion brands including Ronny Kobo, Nununu, Gant, Lee Cooper, and Nine West, alongside studios and photographers running client work. Vendor-published, and broader across brand size and contributor type.

A realistic workflow comparison: buying expertise versus keeping it​

Consider a brand with three lines—womenswear, a kids range, and a small accessories capsule—producing roughly 200 SKUs a season.

On FashionLab, the batch flow handles the womenswear and kids imagery well, and the kids use case is a real strength. Where the model shows its shape is in the account structure and the economics of expertise. Three lines against a plan built around one brand and one project means paid add-ons; a fourth collaborator means another $20 a month; and 200 SKUs at four images is 800 generations, which at roughly $1.10–$1.20 a token is a meaningful token bill before any rejected frame. If the brand does not have a strong prompt-fluent operator, the marketplace answer is to hire one—which works, and which means the brand's creative consistency is a contractor relationship rather than a stored asset.

On Astria, each line gets a brand workspace, the treatment is approved once per line, and the 200 SKUs import from Shopify or Google Drive and run against it. The accessories capsule uses jewelry templates rather than being forced through an apparel flow. Motion for social comes from the same approved stills. When the brand hires an outside art director, that person works in the workspace and the direction stays after the invoice is paid.

The differences that matter most​

A marketplace for AI creative talent — winner: FashionLab​

This is FashionLab's genuine edge and the one concession that matters here. Hiring vetted creative directors, prompt engineers, retouchers, and 3D artists from inside the platform—plus a professional retouching service for polished finishing—solves a real problem: most brands adopting AI production do not yet have the skills in-house. Astria does not offer a labour marketplace. Brands that know they need people as much as software should weigh this seriously.

Owning the direction versus renting it — winner: Astria​

The marketplace solves the skills gap by supplying a person. Astria solves it by making the output of that person durable: once a treatment is approved, running it does not require the expert. Both are legitimate strategies; only one of them costs less next season than it did this one.

Category coverage — winner: Astria​

FashionLab's flow is built around garments on models, with editorial projects as a use case. A jewelry capsule, a beauty extension, or footwear macro work each carry conventions an apparel flow does not encode. Astria treats them as separate template categories.

Casting — winner: Astria, narrowly​

This is closer than most rows in this comparison, and FashionLab deserves credit: a free model library, custom brand models, licensed digital twins, and explicit kids and size-inclusive use cases is a strong set. Astria's advantage is that casting sits alongside locations, poses, and brand references as reusable production assets that persist across seasons, rather than being selected per batch.

Motion — winner: Astria​

We found no video capability in FashionLab's material reviewed. Astria animates approved stills with a choice of current video options inside the same workflow, so social motion carries the campaign's casting and styling.

Account structure and collaboration — winner: Astria​

One brand, one project, and two seats on the entry plan, with paid add-ons for more of each, is a structure that charges for the shape of a real fashion business—multiple lines, several collaborators, a partner agency. Astria's brand workspaces and multiplayer Board with named cursors and live voice are built for that shape rather than metering it.

Collection scale and commercial fit — winner: Astria​

Tokens at roughly $1.10–$1.20 per generation, stacked on a base plan plus per-seat and per-project charges, produce a bill that is difficult to forecast and grows with every rejected frame. Astria treats the collection as the unit of work and prices to usage—pay for what you create. This article makes no claim that Astria is cheaper; it observes that four separate charges are not a production budget. Model a full collection, including rework and all your lines, before comparing.

Compounding production value — winner: Astria​

In Astria, products, avatars, templates, approvals, and outputs accumulate in a workspace shared by the whole production, and the next season starts from them. On FashionLab, what accumulates is a library of generated looks and, if you used the marketplace, a relationship with a freelancer.

Choose FashionLab if...​

  • You need to hire AI creative talent as much as you need software.
  • A professional retouching service inside the platform is valuable to you.
  • Your work centres on batch on-model apparel imagery, including kids and size-inclusive casting.
  • A single brand and project fits your business, or the add-on costs are acceptable.

Choose Astria if...​

  • You want creative direction to become a brand asset rather than a hired service.
  • Multiple lines or brands need their own workspaces without per-project charges.
  • Your categories extend into beauty, jewelry, footwear, sports, or luxury.
  • Social motion should carry the same casting and styling as the campaign.
  • Review should happen on a shared canvas with voice, with your external partners inside it.

The bottom line​

For fashion brands producing a full season, Astria is the stronger choice: broader categories, motion, workspaces that match how brands are actually organised, and a model where the expertise you pay for stays with you. FashionLab has built the most interesting answer to the skills gap in this category, and a brand that knows it needs people as well as tooling should take its marketplace seriously.

The question to settle before choosing: do you want to hire the expertise, or keep it?

What to test before choosing either platform​

Price the whole shape of your business, not the entry plan: count brands, projects, seats, and a realistic annual generation volume including rejected frames. Run five representative SKUs through both, spanning at least two categories and including a kids or extended-size product if relevant, then add a colorway after approval. Ask for social motion derived from an approved still. Have a senior creative review outputs blind for garment fidelity, drape, anatomy, styling, and brand fit. Finally, ask what remains yours if you stop paying.

Frequently asked questions​

Is FashionLab an Astria alternative?​

Yes, for generating on-model fashion imagery in batches. The distinguishing part of FashionLab is its creative marketplace and retouching service; Astria's is producing a whole collection across every channel from one approved treatment.

What is FashionLab's strongest feature?​

Its creative marketplace. Brands can hire AI creative directors, prompt engineers, retouchers, and 3D artists, and an in-built professional retouching service handles polished finishing at scale.

How does FashionLab's pricing scale to a catalog?​

Its entry plan covers one brand and one project with two seats, extra seats and projects are paid add-ons, and tokens run roughly $1.10–$1.20 each. A 60-SKU drop at four images each is a few hundred dollars in tokens before rework.

Do both handle kids and size-inclusive casting?​

Yes — both address them explicitly, and it is a genuine strength of FashionLab's use-case set. Astria additionally carries locations, poses, and brand references as reusable production assets alongside casting.

Is Astria better than FashionLab for fashion brands?​

For producing a collection across channels, yes: broader categories, motion, multi-brand workspaces, and usage-scoped pricing. Brands that want to hire AI creative talent alongside the tooling should look closely at FashionLab's marketplace.

For adjacent decisions, see how Astria compares with Pixelz, Stoodio, and Lookgen.

Sources and methodology​

This article compares public product information available on September 1, 2026. Key sources include FashionLab's homepage describing its five-step batch flow, model library and digital-twin options, published use cases, creative marketplace, and retouching service, and its pricing page covering the Basic plan's brand, project, and seat limits, add-on costs, and token package rates, plus Astria's fashion and ecommerce offering, template gallery, workspace documentation, and video documentation.

Pricing, token rates, plan limits, marketplace scope, and product features can change. Confirm current terms and test representative garments before making a production decision.

item.title: Astria vs Fermat (2026): Which Is Better for Fashion Brands?
item.description: Astria vs Fermat for fashion brands: a design-team AI toolbox with enterprise security versus a production system for catalog, campaign, social, and motion.
item.content:encoded:
Fermat is the generative AI toolbox that fashion and luxury design departments actually buy. Fifty-plus tools spanning sketch to render, design modification, graphic extraction, and outfit visualization, wrapped in a security posture—SOC2 Type II, SSO, on-premise options, private models—that survives a luxury group's procurement review. Its reference list is the strongest design-side evidence in this comparison. Astria is bought by a different department for a different job.

The short answer: Astria is the clear overall winner for producing a collection's imagery across every channel. Choose Fermat when the buyer is the design team and the requirement list starts with security and IP ownership.

How we evaluated Astria and Fermat​

We used six B2B buying questions: which department buys it and for what, whether creative direction persists between uses, casting and channel depth, how collaborators outside the company participate, how a full collection runs, and what the commercial model assumes.

Quick verdict: Astria vs Fermat​

Professional fashion productionPDP and campaign images produced from design assetsBrand-directed production across ecommerce, lookbook, campaign, and socialAstria
Creative directionCustom models trained on brand archives; applied per outputApproved treatment — casting, styling, scene, crop, lighting, format — stored and reusedAstria
Casting and assetsTry designs on different models and settingsModels across ages and body types, including children and extended-size casting, plus locations and posesAstria
Category coverageApparel, prints and graphics, home decorApparel, beauty, jewelry, footwear, sports, luxury, and editorial templatesAstria

Enterprise security and IP postureSOC2 Type II, SSO, on-premise, private models, explicit content ownershipStandard commercial termsFermat
Best fitDesign teams at luxury and large retail groupsFashion brands producing on-brand ecommerce, lookbook, campaign, and social assets across a collectionAstria
OverallAn excellent design-department toolboxThe stronger platform for professional fashion productionAstria

Reviewed August 31, 2026; no controlled image-quality benchmark was run.

Fermat: a toolbox with a procurement-ready wrapper​

Fermat calls itself the generative AI toolbox used by global fashion and luxury brands, and its reference list backs the claim: S.Oliver Group, ASOS, Tendam, PUIG, Desigual, Riachuelo, and Children's Apparel Network. That is a serious set of names, and notably they are fashion names—unlike several general creative platforms whose marquee logos come from other industries.

The product is organized as tools rather than as a workflow. More than fifty of them cover sketch-to-render, parametric design modification, extracting graphics and prints from reference imagery, and visualizing garments on models. For ecommerce work specifically, Fermat describes pulling garments out of styled imagery to produce clean flat-lays, then visualizing on models, adjusting backgrounds and poses, and exporting up to 4K. It publishes efficiency claims of 75–80% reduction on core design tasks and 192× faster outfit visualization; both are vendor figures without disclosed methodology.

The differentiator that closes deals is the wrapper. SOC2 Type II, SSO, on-premise deployment options, private models that do not train on customer data, and an explicit statement that generations belong to the customer. For a luxury group whose archive is the crown jewel, that combination is not a nice-to-have.

Pricing is published, which is welcome: roughly $30 a month for 150 credits at the individual tier, $250 a month for 500 credits with unlimited users at the team tier, and custom enterprise. One credit per image, four per video.

Astria: a professional fashion-production environment​

Astria is organized around producing a collection rather than around a toolkit. Products, casting, references, templates, and outputs live in a brand workspace, and the approved treatment—casting, styling, scene, crop, lighting, format—is the reusable unit.

The difference is what happens on the second SKU. A toolbox applies an operation again; a treatment applies a decision again. Astria's templates cover beauty, jewelry, footwear, sports, luxury, and editorial as distinct categories; the casting library spans ages and body types including children and extended sizes; and campaign, editorial, social, and motion all derive from the same approved direction.

Public proof: design adoption versus production adoption​

Fermat's evidence sits with design departments at large fashion groups, which is exactly where its product is aimed and is genuinely strong. Read it as proof that the toolbox earns a place in a luxury design workflow.

Astria's public materials show a production base among fashion brands and the professionals who create for them: Ronny Kobo, Nununu, Gant, Lee Cooper, and Nine West, alongside studios and photographers running client work. Vendor-published in both cases; the difference is which function inside a brand is doing the adopting.

A realistic workflow comparison: two departments, one collection​

Consider a mid-size group where the design team already uses Fermat and the ecommerce team is choosing how to produce the season's imagery.

The design team's experience is good, and the tools fit how designers work: extract a print from a reference, modify a silhouette, visualize the piece on a model before the sample exists. Credits are cheap per image, security cleared review, and the archive stays private.

Extending that into production is where the shape strains. Producing 250 SKUs across PDP, detail, campaign, and social means running tools repeatedly rather than running an approved treatment; the brand's crop and casting conventions live in whoever operates the tools; casting for the children's line and macro conventions for jewelry are outside the library's depth; and when the freelance art director wants to review, the natural unit is exported files rather than a shared canvas. The 500-credit team tier covers 500 images a month, which a 250-SKU catalog at four images each exceeds in a single push.

With Astria, the ecommerce team defines the treatment once with the art director inside the workspace, imports the SKU set from Shopify or Google Drive, and runs it. Campaign, social, and motion extend the same direction. The design team keeps Fermat, because nothing about this replaces sketch-to-render or print extraction.

The differences that matter most​

Enterprise security and IP posture — winner: Fermat​

This is Fermat's genuine edge and the one concession that matters here. SOC2 Type II, SSO, on-premise options, private models that do not train on customer data, and explicit content ownership form a package that many organizations require before any creative AI tool touches an archive. If your procurement review starts there, Fermat has already answered the hard questions and Astria should be asked to document its own terms.

Toolbox versus treatment — winner: Astria​

Fifty tools is impressive breadth and it puts the burden of consistency on the operator. Every asset is the result of choices made again. Astria stores the choice: the approved treatment produces the next SKU the same way as the last one, without anyone remembering how.

Channel coverage across the season — winner: Astria​

Fermat's ecommerce use case produces PDP and campaign images from design assets. A season also needs lookbook, editorial, social-native crops, and motion, consistent with one another. Astria treats those as expressions of a single direction rather than as separate tool runs.

Casting depth — winner: Astria​

Trying designs on different models is a design-validation feature. Production casting is a different requirement: consistent identities across a collection, age ranges including children, extended-size representation, and locations and poses that recur across seasons. Astria's library is built for that.

Collaboration on the creative decision — winner: Astria​

Fermat's team tier is generous—unlimited users—and the interaction model is still tool-and-asset. Astria's multiplayer Board is built for the moment a look gets approved: named cursors, live voice, and the production canvas shared with the photographer, in-house studio, and agency.

Collection scale and commercial fit — winner: Astria​

Credits per image are transparent and easy to reason about, and the published team tier tops out at 500 images a month before enterprise. That suits design exploration and constrains catalog production, where rework is routine. Astria treats the collection as the unit of work and prices to usage—pay for what you create. This article makes no claim about which is cheaper; the meters measure different work. Model a full collection, including rework, before comparing.

Compounding production value — winner: Astria​

In Astria, products, avatars, templates, approvals, and outputs accumulate in a shared workspace, and the next season starts from them. In Fermat, what accumulates is a brand-trained model and a body of design assets — valuable upstream, and not a production workflow.

Choose Fermat if...​

  • The buyer is the design department and the work is design: sketch to render, prints, modification.
  • SOC2 Type II, SSO, on-premise, or private-model requirements gate any tool you adopt.
  • Protecting a brand archive from training use is a stated condition.
  • Published per-credit pricing at design-scale volumes fits your usage.

Choose Astria if...​

  • The buyer is the team producing the season's imagery.
  • One approved creative direction must carry across catalog, lookbook, campaign, social, and motion.
  • Casting depth across ages and body types is a production requirement.
  • Your photographer, studio, or agency should work inside the brand workspace.
  • Catalog volumes exceed what design-scale credit tiers comfortably cover.

The bottom line​

These two are more complementary than competitive, and the split runs along departmental lines. Fermat is an excellent toolbox for a design team, with the security posture a luxury group needs. Astria is the stronger choice for producing the collection's imagery: it stores the creative decision, covers every channel, and scales to a catalog rather than to design exploration.

If your design team already runs Fermat, that is not an argument against Astria. It is an argument for asking which department has the bottleneck.

What to test before choosing either platform​

Run five representative SKUs through both to a full channel set — PDP, detail, campaign, social — and add a colorway after approval. Count credits consumed including rejected frames, and check that number against your real catalog volume. Ask both vendors for written security and IP terms. Have a senior creative review outputs blind for garment fidelity, drape, anatomy, styling, and brand fit. Finally, ask a second operator to reproduce the approved direction.

Is Fermat an Astria alternative?​

Partly. Fermat is a generative toolbox bought by design departments — sketch to render, design modification, graphic extraction, outfit visualization. Astria is bought by the people producing the collection's imagery for every channel.

What is Fermat's strongest advantage?​

Enterprise security and IP posture: SOC2 Type II, SSO, on-premise options, private models that do not train on customer data, and explicit content ownership — backed by luxury and large-retail references.

Which one does the ecommerce team buy?​

Astria, generally. Fermat's centre of gravity is the design department and its 50+ tools. Astria is organised around producing and approving a collection's imagery across catalog, lookbook, campaign, social, and motion.

How do the pricing models differ?​

Fermat publishes credit plans — around $30 a month for individuals and $250 for teams, with one credit per image. Astria's brand pricing is scoped to usage. Model a full collection, including rework, before comparing.

Is Astria better than Fermat for fashion brands?​

For producing a collection's imagery, yes: deeper casting, full channel coverage, and collaborative review with external partners. Design departments with strict security requirements and a tool-based workflow should evaluate Fermat.

Pletor: an engine for campaign versions​

Pletor's framing is deliberate: production infrastructure, not a generative toy. It orchestrates models—Flux, Seedance, Kling, Veo, Sora, and language models among them, with new ones added continuously—alongside brand context and marketing data, so a team can produce product imagery from a catalog, performance ads at campaign pace, and AI-generated UGC. The clearest statement of intent is its promise to turn one campaign into every version it needs to be: languages, formats, markets, seasons.

Pricing is published and legible: Starter at $19 a month for 1,000 credits, Builder at $49 for 3,000 with a month of rollover, Studio at $199 for 15,000 with three months of rollover and an onboarding call, plus annual discounts and enterprise. All plans include unlimited team invites, which is unusually generous in this category and worth noting.

Its published references—an agency, a creative director, a global consumer electronics brand—describe marketing organizations rather than fashion brands. That is consistent with the positioning. Pletor is not claiming to be a fashion product, and a fair comparison should not pretend otherwise.

Astria: a professional fashion-production environment​

Astria produces the source material. Products, casting, references, templates, and outputs live in a brand workspace, and the approved treatment—casting, styling, scene, crop, lighting, format—is the reusable unit that generates the collection's imagery.

That includes fashion knowledge a general marketing engine has no reason to carry: category templates for beauty, jewelry, footwear, sports, luxury, and editorial work; a casting library spanning ages and body types, including children and extended-size casting; product references and a refinement pass aimed at how garments and faces actually read. Campaign frames and social crops extend the same approved direction, and motion animates stills the brand already signed off.

Public proof: marketing adoption versus fashion production​

Pletor's evidence points at marketing teams and agencies, with a named agency case study and a consumer electronics reference. Read as evidence for ad production infrastructure, that is reasonable and on-point.

Astria's public materials show a production base among fashion brands and the professionals who create for them: Ronny Kobo, Nununu, Gant, Lee Cooper, and Nine West, alongside studios and photographers running client work. Vendor-published in both cases, from different industries.

A realistic workflow comparison: where the campaign starts​

Consider a fashion brand launching a 90-piece spring collection with a significant paid-social budget. The growth team needs dozens of ad variants across three markets and two languages. The ecommerce team needs PDP sets. The brand team needs a lookbook and campaign imagery.

Pletor is excellent at one third of this, and it is the third that comes last. Versioning a campaign across formats, markets, and languages is precisely its design goal, and its credit pricing makes high variant counts affordable. But every one of those variants derives from source creative: a cast model wearing the garment, shot in a treatment the brand approved. If that source does not exist, no amount of versioning infrastructure creates it, and generic product imagery generated from a catalog is not the same as a campaign image a brand would run.

Astria produces the source. Casting, styling, lighting, crop, and format get approved once and applied across the 90 pieces imported from Shopify or Google Drive; the lookbook and campaign frames come from the same treatment; motion extends approved stills. The growth team then has something worth versioning—and can version it in Pletor, or anywhere else, without conflict.

The differences that matter most​

Ad variant production at campaign pace — winner: Pletor​

This is Pletor's genuine edge and the one concession that matters here. Producing many versions of an approved campaign across languages, formats, markets, and seasons is a real operational problem for growth teams, and Pletor is built for it with pricing and rollover that suit bursty demand. Astria is not competing for that job, and a brand with a large paid-social operation may well want both.

Fashion knowledge — winner: Astria​

A general marketing engine has no opinion about drape, casting conventions, or how a jewelry macro differs from an apparel PDP, because it serves electronics and services too. Astria's templates and casting library exist because those conventions are worth encoding once. When the output is a garment on a person, supplied domain knowledge beats general flexibility.

Casting depth — winner: Astria​

Pletor generates people as part of an output. Astria treats casting as a production asset: a reusable library across ages and body types, including children and extended-size casting, that persists between seasons and stays consistent across a collection.

Where the creative decision lives — winner: Astria​

Feeding brand context into an orchestration system produces outputs that are approximately on-brand. Storing an approved treatment produces outputs that are consistent because consistency is the object being stored, not an instruction repeated per asset.

Review and creative collaboration — winner: Astria​

Pletor's collaboration model is generous on access—unlimited team invites—and oriented toward marketing workflow. Astria's multiplayer Board is oriented toward the creative decision: named cursors, live voice, and the production canvas shared with the photographer, in-house studio, and agency.

Collection scale — winner: Astria​

Pletor's credits are sized around ad output; Studio's 15,000 monthly credits translate to a few thousand images, which is generous for campaign variants and a different shape from a catalog run. Astria imports the whole SKU set and runs it against the approved treatment, then extends into campaign, editorial, social, and motion.

Commercial model for brands — winner: Astria​

Credit tiers with rollover are a sensible fit for campaign bursts and an awkward one for a season's production, where volume is predictable but revision-heavy and the unit that matters is a finished collection rather than a variant count. Astria's brand pricing is scoped to usage—pay for what you create. No claim is made here that Astria is cheaper; the two meters measure different work. Model a full collection, including rework, before comparing.

Compounding production value — winner: Astria​

In Astria, products, avatars, templates, approvals, and outputs accumulate, and next season starts from them. In Pletor, what accumulates is a library of campaign variants — valuable while the campaign runs, and superseded when the next one starts.

Choose Pletor if...​

  • Your bottleneck is ad variant volume across formats, markets, and languages.
  • You are a marketing or growth team rather than a production team.
  • Published credit pricing with rollover suits your bursty demand.
  • Your source creative already exists and needs multiplying, not making.

Choose Astria if...​

  • You need to produce the collection imagery that campaigns are built from.
  • Fashion-specific casting, categories, and garment handling matter.
  • One approved creative direction must carry across catalog, lookbook, campaign, social, and motion.
  • Your photographer, studio, and agency should work in the same brand workspace.
  • Review should happen on a shared canvas with voice, not in a marketing workflow tool.

The bottom line​

These two are complementary far more than they are competitive, and the honest advice is to be clear about which problem you have. If you cannot produce enough ad variants, Pletor solves that well. If your ads are constrained by not having enough good source imagery of your own collection, a versioning engine will not help — and Astria is the stronger choice.

What to test before choosing either platform​

Ask one question first: do we lack variants, or do we lack source creative? Then test accordingly. For Astria, run five representative SKUs through a full channel set — PDP, detail, campaign, social — and add a colorway after approval. For Pletor, take one approved campaign image and count how many usable market and format versions come out of it. Have a senior creative review outputs blind for garment fidelity, drape, anatomy, styling, and brand fit.

Frequently asked questions​

Is Pletor an Astria alternative?​

Only partly. Pletor is creative infrastructure for marketing teams — performance ads, UGC, and campaign versioning across markets and formats. Astria is a fashion production system for catalog, lookbook, campaign, and social imagery.

Is Pletor built for fashion?​

No. It serves marketing teams across industries, and its published customer references span agencies and consumer electronics. Fashion is a use case rather than the design center.

Which is better for paid-social ad volume?​

Pletor. Turning one campaign into every version it needs — languages, formats, markets, seasons — at campaign pace is exactly what it is built for, and it publishes credit-based pricing to match.

Which produces the assets the ads are built from?​

Astria. Casting, styling, and product imagery for the collection come first; ad versioning is downstream of them. Astria produces that source material from one approved creative direction.

Is Astria better than Pletor for fashion brands?​

For producing a fashion collection's imagery, yes. Marketing teams whose bottleneck is ad variant volume rather than source imagery should evaluate Pletor for that job.

For adjacent decisions, see how Astria compares with Tolstoy, FLORA, and Figma Weave.

Sources and methodology​

This article compares public product information available on August 29, 2026. Key sources include Pletor's homepage describing its orchestration approach, supported models, and marketing use cases, its published customer references, and its pricing page covering credit tiers, rollover, and team access, plus Astria's fashion and ecommerce offering, template gallery, workspace documentation, and video documentation.

item.description: Astria vs Stoodio for fashion brands: licensed real-model digital twins and guided onboarding versus a self-directed production workspace built for collections.
item.content:encoded:
Stoodio is one of the few competitors in this set that is, like Astria, built exclusively for fashion—image generation, video, workflows, a model database, and asset management in one platform. Its distinguishing bet is legal: a partnership with ModelManagement.com giving access to a very large pool of consented, commercially licensed real-model digital twins. The question for a buyer is whether that licensing advantage outweighs a production model that runs through the vendor.

The short answer: Astria is the clear overall winner for most fashion brands—broader categories, deeper casting, live collaborative review, and no onboarding engagement to get started. Choose Stoodio when licensed real-model likeness is the overriding requirement.

Quick verdict: Astria vs Stoodio​

OverallA strong licensing-led fashion studioThe stronger platform for professional fashion productionAstria

Reviewed August 29, 2026; no controlled image-quality benchmark was run.

Stoodio: licensing as the product strategy​

Stoodio's pitch is that it builds a brand's AI studio, and it is refreshingly specific about being fashion-only rather than a general image tool. The platform lists five integrated capabilities: image generation, video generation, workflows that chain prompts, models, edits, and exports into repeatable pipelines, a model database, and asset management.

The model database is the strategy. As an official partner of ModelManagement.com, Stoodio offers access to over 100,000 consented digital twins with worldwide, perpetual commercial rights, and it is pointed about what that means—no composite faces, no grey zones. For a brand whose legal team is uneasy about synthetic likeness, or that operates in a market tightening around AI disclosure and personality rights, this is a materially different proposition from a library of invented faces.

The company frames itself as a production partner rather than a tool, promising guided onboarding so a team integrates AI into real production from the first session. Its published evidence is a single detailed case study: a Berlin activewear brand reporting 40% lower cost per SKU, production cycles moving from three weeks to three days, and double the content output. There is no published pricing; the route in is a booked demo.

Astria: a professional fashion-production environment​

Astria shares Stoodio's fashion focus and diverges on autonomy and breadth. Products, casting, references, templates, and outputs live in a brand workspace, and the approved treatment—casting, styling, scene, crop, lighting, format—is the reusable unit the brand's own people edit and run.

Breadth shows in two places. Categories: templates treat beauty, jewelry, footwear, sports, luxury, and editorial as distinct fashion disciplines, not variations on apparel. And casting: alongside adult models across body types, the library covers children's and extended-size casting, which are production requirements a licensed adult-model roster does not address.

Public proof: one deep story versus a broader base​

Stoodio's case study is genuinely useful—specific numbers, a named founder, a real brand—and it is one story from a small brand. That is honest early-stage evidence, and a buyer should read it as such rather than as a pattern.

Astria's public materials show a production base among fashion brands and the professionals who create for them: Ronny Kobo, Nununu, Gant, Lee Cooper, and Nine West, alongside studios and photographers running client work. Also vendor-published, and broader across brand size and contributor type.

A realistic workflow comparison: the legal review​

Consider a European brand whose counsel has flagged AI-generated faces as a risk. The marketing director wants AI production; legal wants documented consent and clear commercial rights for any human likeness used in advertising.

This is Stoodio's scenario, and it answers it well. A licensed twin from a consented roster with worldwide perpetual rights is a document legal can read, and the onboarding engagement means someone from the vendor helps wire it into the brand's real production. If that constraint is genuinely binding, the rest of this comparison is secondary.

Now change one detail: the brand also sells a children's line and a small jewelry capsule, and its campaign imagery is set by a freelance stylist who is not an employee. The licensed adult-model roster does not cover the children's line. Jewelry needs different lighting and macro conventions than activewear. And the stylist needs to be inside the workflow, reviewing looks with the team, not briefing a vendor. In Astria those are ordinary: children's and extended-size casting exist in the library, jewelry and beauty are first-class template categories, and the stylist joins the brand workspace and reviews on the multiplayer Board with live voice.

The differences that matter most​

Model licensing and consent — winner: Stoodio​

This is Stoodio's genuine edge and the one concession that matters here. A roster of over 100,000 consented real-model digital twins, sourced through a named partner with worldwide perpetual commercial rights, is the cleanest answer to likeness risk in this comparison, and Astria does not match it. Brands operating under strict legal review, or in markets tightening around AI disclosure and personality rights, should weight this heavily and ask both vendors for written rights documentation.

Getting started without an engagement — winner: Astria​

Stoodio's positioning as a production partner with guided onboarding is a real service, and it is also a dependency and a delay. Astria is used directly by brands and by the studios, photographers, and educators who serve them, which means a team can validate the workflow on its own products before committing to anything.

Casting breadth beyond licensed adults — winner: Astria​

A licensed twin roster solves adult likeness elegantly and does not solve children's casting or extended-size representation, both of which are ordinary production requirements for brands with a full line. Astria's library covers ages and body types, including children and extended-size casting, alongside locations and poses.

Category coverage — winner: Astria​

Stoodio's published channels—ecommerce, campaign, social, print—describe distribution rather than category. Astria's templates encode the conventions of beauty, jewelry, footwear, sports, luxury, and editorial work, which is what a brand with more than one product type actually needs.

Review and external collaborators — winner: Astria​

Stoodio offers asset management: organize, review, and ship from one place. That is the right feature set for tracking output. Astria's multiplayer Board is for making the decision: named cursors, live voice, and the production canvas shared with the photographer, the in-house studio, and the agency.

Collection scale and commercial fit — winner: Astria​

Both build repeatable pipelines. Astria's differ in where the collection enters: the SKU set imports from Shopify or Google Drive and runs against the approved treatment, then extends into campaign, editorial, social, and motion. On commercials, Stoodio publishes no pricing, so a brand cannot model a season before entering a sales conversation; Astria's brand pricing is scoped to usage—pay for what you create. This article makes no claim that Astria is cheaper; it notes that one option can be estimated against a real collection before commitment and the other cannot.

Compounding production value — winner: Astria​

In Astria, products, avatars, templates, approvals, and outputs accumulate in a workspace the whole production shares, and the next season starts from them. Stoodio's pipelines accumulate too—inside a partnership the brand does not fully operate alone.

Choose Stoodio if...​

  • Documented consent and commercial rights for human likeness are a hard legal requirement.
  • You want a vendor partner to help integrate AI into production from the first session.
  • Adult apparel is the bulk of your line.
  • A licensed real-model roster matters more to you than running the workflow independently.

Choose Astria if...​

  • You want to validate the workflow on your own products before any commitment.
  • Your line spans categories — beauty, jewelry, footwear, sports, luxury, editorial — and age ranges including children.
  • External stylists, photographers, or agencies should work inside the brand workspace.
  • Review should happen on a shared canvas with voice, not through an asset manager.
  • One approved creative direction must carry across the collection and every channel.

The bottom line​

For most fashion brands, Astria is the stronger choice: broader categories, deeper casting, collaborative review with the people who actually set the look, and a workflow the brand runs itself. Stoodio has built the best licensing answer in this category, and for a brand where consent documentation is the binding constraint, that may be the only factor that matters.

Ask both vendors for their rights documentation in writing. Then ask who runs the workflow after onboarding ends.

What to test before choosing either platform​

Run five representative SKUs through both, spanning at least two categories if your line has them, and include a children's or extended-size product if relevant. Require PDP, detail, campaign, and social crops, then add a colorway after approval. Request written likeness-rights documentation from both. Have a senior creative review outputs blind for garment fidelity, drape, anatomy, styling, and brand fit. Finally, invite your external stylist or photographer into the workflow and see whether they can work in it.

Yes — it is a genuine fashion-specific competitor with image generation, video, workflows, a model database, and asset management. The main differences are its licensing-led model library, its demo-and-onboarding sales motion, and how much of the work you run yourself.

What is Stoodio's strongest advantage?​

Consent and licensing. Through its ModelManagement.com partnership Stoodio offers a very large pool of commercially licensed real-model digital twins with worldwide, perpetual rights — a clean answer for brands with legal sensitivity about AI faces.

Which can a brand start using on its own?​

Astria. Stoodio's route is a booked demo with guided onboarding and positions itself as a production partner. Astria is used directly by brands and by the studios, photographers, and educators producing for them.

How does published proof compare?​

Stoodio publishes one detailed customer story with specific outcomes. Astria's materials name several fashion brands plus studios and photographers running client work. Both are vendor-published rather than independent.

Is Astria better than Stoodio for fashion brands?​

For most brands, yes: broader category templates, deeper casting including children and extended sizes, live multiplayer review, and no onboarding engagement required. Brands whose overriding requirement is licensed real-model likeness should evaluate Stoodio on that basis.

item.content:encoded:
Aiuta is an enterprise virtual try-on company first. Its shopper experience is deployed at recognizable retailers, and Aiuta Studio is a second product that returns finished product photography after human QA. If you are already buying try-on from Aiuta, the studio looks like an easy consolidation. It is worth understanding what you would be consolidating into.

The short answer: Astria is the clear overall winner for fashion brands producing and directing their own imagery. Choose Aiuta when shopper-facing try-on is the primary purchase and catalog imagery delivered as a service is a welcome extra.

Professional fashion productionProduct photography with backgrounds, lighting, and flat-lay conversionBrand-directed production across ecommerce, lookbook, campaign, and socialAstria

Casting and assetsDiverse AI models offered by the platformModels across ages and body types, including children and extended-size casting, plus locations and posesAstria

Campaign and editorial workNot the studio's focus in the material reviewedCampaign, editorial, and social treatments from the same approved setupAstria

Reviewed August 28, 2026; no controlled image-quality benchmark was run.

Aiuta: try-on infrastructure, with a studio attached​

Aiuta's core business is shopper-facing virtual try-on for enterprise retail. Shoppers upload a photo and see themselves in an item in seconds, building single looks or complete outfits. It deploys via SDK or API and is designed to slot into existing ecommerce infrastructure with minimal engineering lift. The customer list is the strongest part of the story: ASOS, About You, Alice + Olivia, adidas Originals, Namshi, HEMCO, Tanya Taylor, and Leset.

Aiuta Studio is the second product and works differently from most tools in this comparison. A brand supplies basic product images; the platform returns studio-grade outputs with custom backgrounds and lighting, including flat-lay conversion from model shots. Two details define the experience: every output passes human QA before delivery, with a stated 95% first-pass acceptance rate, and turnaround is quoted at 24–48 hours.

That QA guarantee is a real differentiator against pure self-serve generators, and it is also the shape of a service. You submit, you wait, you receive. Neither Aiuta page we reviewed publishes pricing for Studio.

Astria: a professional fashion-production environment​

Astria puts the creative decision inside the brand. Products, casting, references, templates, and outputs live in a brand workspace, and the approved treatment—casting, styling, scene, crop, lighting, format—is stored, editable, and reusable by the people who own the brand's look.

The immediate consequence is iteration speed. A creative director who wants a warmer background, a tighter crop, or different casting changes the treatment and re-runs; there is no submission and no return cycle. The second consequence is coverage: templates span beauty, jewelry, footwear, sports, luxury, and editorial alongside apparel, and the same direction extends into campaign frames, social crops, and motion.

Public proof: retail deployment versus production adoption​

Aiuta's evidence is enterprise retail try-on, and it is genuinely impressive at that: recognizable global retailers running its shopper experience. We found no named customer references specifically for Aiuta Studio in the material reviewed, and no published performance metrics on the shopper-experience page beyond capability claims.

Astria's public materials show a production base among fashion brands and the professionals who create for them: Ronny Kobo, Nununu, Gant, Lee Cooper, and Nine West, alongside studios and photographers running client work. Vendor-published in both cases. The relevant question is which body of evidence matches the job you are buying for.

A realistic workflow comparison: the consolidation temptation​

Consider a retailer already running Aiuta try-on across its apparel catalog. The ecommerce director likes the vendor, the integration is stable, and Studio promises catalog imagery from the same contract. Consolidating suppliers is a legitimately good instinct.

Here is how the season plays out. Product images go in; polished outputs come back within 24–48 hours, QA-checked, and the acceptance rate is high. Then the creative director sees the first batch and wants the crop 15% wider and the light cooler. That is a new submission and another cycle. Two weeks later a campaign brief lands that needs editorial framing rather than catalog framing, and that is outside what the studio product is aimed at. The lookbook needs a different answer again. The consolidation saved a vendor relationship and did not save the production.

With Astria, the crop change is an edit to the approved treatment, applied instantly across everything already produced and everything still to come. The campaign frames and lookbook come from the same treatment rather than a different supplier. And the try-on integration—if the retailer wants it—stays exactly where it is, doing the job it is genuinely good at.

The differences that matter most​

Enterprise shopper-facing try-on — winner: Aiuta​

This is Aiuta's genuine edge and the one concession that matters here. Rendering a specific shopper into a garment in seconds, deployed at ASOS and adidas Originals scale, with SDK and API integration paths, is hard infrastructure that Astria does not build. Retailers whose bottleneck is fit confidence at the point of purchase should evaluate Aiuta on those merits and not expect a production tool to substitute.

Who holds the creative decision — winner: Astria​

A QA-checked delivery pipeline is dependable precisely because it is standardized, and standardization is the opposite of art direction. In Astria the treatment is the brand's object: editable by the brand's creative director, visible to the brand's team, and applied on the brand's schedule.

Iteration speed — winner: Astria​

A 24–48 hour turnaround is excellent for a service and slow for a decision. Creative work converges through rapid, cheap iteration; a delivery cycle makes each iteration a scheduled event. This is the single biggest practical difference between buying finished images and running production.

Coverage of the season — winner: Astria​

Aiuta Studio is aimed at product photography. A season also needs lookbook, campaign, editorial, social, and motion, all sharing one visual language. Astria produces those from a single approved direction, which is both fewer suppliers and a more coherent result.

Casting depth — winner: Astria​

Aiuta advertises diverse AI models intended to reflect a brand's customers, which is the right ambition. Astria's reusable library goes further into production requirements: ages and body types, including children and extended-size casting, alongside locations, poses, and brand references that persist across seasons.

FLORA: a creative canvas that reaches into fashion​

FLORA describes itself as the AI-powered canvas for designers, brand teams, and agencies, and it has built a genuine fashion solution on top of that foundation. The pitch for fashion teams is end to end: from a sketch to a render, through colorways and fabrics, to on-model and campaign imagery, with batch application of one approved look across every SKU. It splits the experience into a Fashion Studio for everyday work and a Canvas for deeper ideation where models and steps chain together into reusable workflows.

The platform breadth is real: FLORA advertises access to 50+ models spanning image, video, and multimodal reasoning under one subscription, with recognizable video models available for cinematic work. It has raised $42 million and its published references include Pentagram, Lionsgate, Base Design, and Hebbia.

That reference list is the most useful signal for a fashion buyer. Pentagram is a design consultancy; Lionsgate is entertainment; Hebbia is enterprise software. They are impressive names and they attest to FLORA's quality as a creative environment. What the fashion solution page offers instead of brand case studies is credits to individual designers. For a brand evaluating who has actually run a season on the platform, that is a thinner evidence base than the platform's overall profile suggests.

Astria: a professional fashion-production environment​

Astria is deliberately less ambitious in scope and more specific in depth. Products, casting, references, templates, and outputs live in a brand workspace, and the approved treatment—casting, styling, scene, crop, lighting, format—is the reusable unit that produces the season.

Depth shows in the assets. The casting library spans ages and body types, including children and extended-size casting, alongside locations, poses, and brand references that accumulate season over season. Templates treat beauty, jewelry, footwear, sports, luxury, and editorial as distinct fashion categories rather than variations on apparel. And the collaboration model assumes the work crosses company boundaries, because in fashion it almost always does.

Astria's public materials show a production base among fashion brands and the professionals who create for them: Ronny Kobo, Nununu, Gant, Lee Cooper, and Nine West, alongside studios and photographers running client work. Both sets are vendor-published adoption signals rather than independent benchmarks. The difference is which industry they come from.

A realistic workflow comparison: the season, from sketch to shipped​

Consider a contemporary label developing a 120-piece resort collection. The design team explores silhouettes and prints in the autumn; the production team needs catalog, lookbook, campaign, and social assets in the spring; a freelance photographer sets the visual direction; an agency handles paid social.

FLORA is genuinely strong in the autumn half. Sketch-to-render, colorway exploration, and print and pattern replacement are exactly the design-stage problems a creative team has, and having 50+ models on one canvas makes exploration cheap. The spring half is where the shape of the product starts to matter. Batch across SKUs exists, but the casting depth is shallower, category templates outside apparel are thinner, and—most practically—every additional collaborator is a seat. With self-serve tiers capped at eight seats and per-seat prices running from $18 to $200 a month plus metered usage on top, adding the photographer, two agency people, and a merchandiser is a procurement decision rather than an invitation.

Astria inverts the emphasis. It contributes little to the autumn exploration, and it is built for the spring: the approved treatment runs across the 120 pieces imported from Shopify or Google Drive, campaign and social extend the same direction, motion animates approved stills, and the photographer and agency work inside the brand workspace rather than against a seat count.

Design-stage ideation — winner: FLORA​

This is FLORA's genuine edge and the one concession that matters here. Sketch to render, colorway and fabric exploration, print and pattern replacement, and very broad model access make it a strong environment for developing what a collection should look like before it exists. Astria does not compete for that work. Design teams whose central problem is exploration should weigh this heavily.

Fashion-specific depth — winner: Astria​

Beyond apparel, fashion production is beauty, jewelry, footwear, sports, luxury, and editorial, each with its own conventions of lighting, crop, and styling. Astria treats those as first-class templates. Casting depth matters just as much: age range, body type, children's and extended-size casting are production requirements, not preferences, and a general on-model capability does not cover them.

Who gets to be in the room — winner: Astria​

This is where per-seat licensing quietly shapes the work. Fashion production is collaborative across company lines—photographer, in-house studio, agency, merchandiser—and a model that charges per seat and caps self-serve teams at eight makes each additional participant a cost decision. Astria's brand workspaces are built for that cast of collaborators, with a multiplayer Board, named cursors, and live voice over the actual looks.

Evidence in your own industry — winner: Astria​

Both companies publish first-party proof. FLORA's strongest names come from design and entertainment; Astria's come from fashion brands and the studios that serve them. Neither is an independent benchmark, and a buyer should discount both accordingly—but when the question is "has anyone run a fashion season on this," the relevant evidence is the fashion evidence.

Collection scale — winner: Astria​

FLORA batches one approved look across SKUs, which is the right idea. Astria imports the SKU set directly from Shopify or Google Drive and runs the approved treatment across it, then extends the same direction into campaign, editorial, social, and motion. The difference is how much of the season comes out of one decision.

Commercial model for brands — winner: Astria​

FLORA's shape is a creative-suite subscription: per seat, per month, with metered usage credits layered on and enterprise beyond the eight-seat ceiling. That is coherent for a design department with stable headcount, and awkward for a production that expands and contracts around a season and pulls in outside collaborators. Astria's brand pricing is scoped to usage—pay for what you create. This article makes no claim that Astria is cheaper; it observes that seats plus credits is not a production budget. Model a full collection, including every collaborator who needs access, before comparing.

Compounding production value — winner: Astria​

In Astria, products, avatars, templates, approvals, and outputs accumulate in a workspace the whole production shares, and next season starts from them. In FLORA, saved workflows accumulate on the canvas—useful, and tied to the seats that can open them.

Choose FLORA if...​

  • Design-stage exploration is the work: silhouettes, colorways, prints, fabrics.
  • You want very broad model access, including video, under one subscription.
  • Your team is a design studio or agency with stable seat count.

Choose Astria if...​

  • Categories beyond apparel — beauty, jewelry, footwear, sports, luxury, editorial — are part of the line.

The bottom line​

These two are complementary more often than they are rivals, and the split is the calendar. FLORA is a strong place to decide what the collection should look like. Astria is the stronger place to produce it once that is decided—deeper fashion assets, no seat gate on the people who make the work, and evidence from the industry you are actually in.

What to test before choosing either platform​

Split the test by stage. For exploration, try a print and colorway development pass on both. For production, run five representative SKUs—including one non-apparel item if your line has them—through a full channel set, then add a colorway after approval. Count the seats the real production needs, external collaborators included, and price that honestly. Have a senior creative review outputs blind for garment fidelity, drape, anatomy, styling, and brand fit. Finally, ask each vendor for a fashion brand reference you can speak to.

Astria. FLORA's marquee references are design and entertainment names such as Pentagram and Lionsgate, and its fashion page credits individual designers. Astria's materials name fashion brands including Ronny Kobo, Gant, Lee Cooper, and Nine West.

FLORA. Sketch-to-render, colorway exploration, and print or pattern replacement are genuine design-stage strengths, backed by very broad model access under one subscription.

Is Astria better than FLORA for fashion brands?​

Figma Weave—the product formerly known as Weavy, acquired by Figma in October 2025—is one of the most capable AI creative environments available: a node-based canvas where many current models sit alongside professional editing tools, inside the design platform creative teams already live in. It is also general-purpose by design. Astria is the opposite bet: a system that already knows what a fashion collection is.

Figma Weave: a canvas for building creative pipelines​

Figma acquired Weavy on October 30, 2025 and relaunched it as Figma Weave. The product's premise, in Figma's own framing, is that the first prompt is a creative starting point rather than a final destination—so generation and hands-on craft belong in the same place.

In practice that means a node-based canvas where outputs from many current models can be combined, branched, and refined, with professional editing operations—inpaint, outpaint, relight, upscale, crop, masking, color work—applied as part of the graph rather than in a separate tool. Model coverage is deliberately broad across image, video, and 3D. Workflows are reusable: a author builds the graph once, and Figma Weave can generate a simplified interface so teammates can run it without touching the nodes. Since 2026 a set of Weave tools and community workflows has been reachable directly inside Figma Design.

It is genuinely excellent software. It is also, by intent, a general creative environment—the published examples span ad generation, product photography, illustration, storyboarding, and 3D rendering. Nothing in it is specifically about fashion.

Astria: a professional fashion-production environment​

Astria makes the opposite trade. Instead of a canvas that can express any workflow, it supplies a workflow that already understands fashion: products, casting, references, templates, and outputs in a brand workspace, with the approved treatment—casting, styling, scene, crop, lighting, format—as the reusable unit.

The practical difference is what you start with. A fashion template for footwear, jewelry, beauty, or editorial work already encodes the conventions of that category. A casting library already spans ages and body types, including children and extended-size casting. The SKU set imports from Shopify or Google Drive rather than being wired up. Astria's Describe tool can extract usable direction from a rights-cleared reference while accounting for products and models already loaded. None of that is a node graph anyone had to author.

Public proof: creative breadth versus fashion production​

Figma Weave's evidence is its adoption across creative disciplines—independent creatives, startups, and enterprise teams including architects, VFX artists, marketers, and designers—and the credibility of the Figma platform around it. That is a strong signal for general creative production and says nothing specific about fashion catalogs.

Astria's public materials show a production base among fashion brands and the professionals who create for them: Ronny Kobo, Nununu, Gant, Lee Cooper, and Nine West, alongside studios and photographers running client work. Vendor-published, and narrow on purpose.

A realistic workflow comparison: who builds the pipeline​

Consider a brand with 200 SKUs, a small creative team, and a design lead who is fluent in Figma.

The Figma Weave path is attractive because the design lead can build exactly what the brand wants: a graph that takes a product photo, places it on a generated model, applies the brand's lighting treatment, produces four crops, and upscales. Once built, the team can run it behind a simplified interface. The costs are real but easy to overlook. Someone has to design that graph and keep it working; the fashion judgment inside it—how this brand casts, how a knit should fall, what crop convention the PDP uses—is knowledge the graph author supplies, not knowledge the tool contributes; and every new category, a jewelry capsule, say, is a new graph. When the design lead leaves, the pipeline becomes an artifact nobody fully understands.

The Astria path starts further along. The team picks a fashion template appropriate to the category, loads the products, sets casting and styling, approves the treatment, and runs the SKU set imported from Shopify or Google Drive. What the brand maintains is a creative decision, not a piece of software. When someone new arrives, they inherit an approved treatment rather than a graph.

The differences that matter most​

Supplied knowledge versus built knowledge — winner: Astria​

This is the whole comparison. A node canvas is infinitely expressive and completely uninformed: it will happily build a beautiful pipeline that gets a garment's drape wrong, because nothing in it knows what drape is. Astria's templates, casting library, and product-reference handling exist because fashion has conventions worth encoding once. Flexibility is valuable when your outputs are unpredictable; supplied domain knowledge is valuable when they are not.

Model breadth and editing craft on one canvas — winner: Figma Weave​

This is Figma Weave's genuine edge and the one concession that matters here. Combining many current models with professional editing operations—relight, inpaint, matte work, compositing—inside a single node graph, reachable from the design environment a team already uses, is a real capability advantage for creative work in general. Teams whose output spans ads, illustration, motion design, and product imagery will get more from that breadth than from any fashion-specific system, and they should choose accordingly.

Who can run it without help — winner: Astria​

Figma Weave's answer is thoughtful: workflow authors can publish a simplified UI so teammates run the graph without editing nodes. But that still divides the team into people who can change the workflow and people who cannot. In Astria, changing the crop convention or the casting is an edit to the treatment, made by the person who owns the creative decision.

Coverage of a fashion season — winner: Astria​

A season is catalog, detail, lookbook, campaign, editorial, social, and motion, produced consistently across a collection. Figma Weave can produce every one of those as an individual asset. Astria produces them as expressions of one approved direction, which is what makes them look like a collection rather than a set of executions.

Collection scale — winner: Astria​

Both scale, differently. Figma Weave scales a workflow once the workflow exists. Astria scales a creative decision: import the SKU set, run it against the approved treatment, extend into campaign and motion. The distinction matters most when the direction changes mid-season—an edit to a template versus a revision to a graph.

Commercial model for brands — winner: Astria​

Figma Weave consumption sits inside Figma's credit and plan structure, which is designed for a design organization rather than for a collection's production budget. Astria's brand pricing is scoped to usage—pay for what you create, sized to the production. No claim is made here that Astria is cheaper; the point is that credits inside a design-seat subscription are a hard thing to map onto 200 SKUs across four channels. Model a full collection, including rework, before comparing.

Compounding production value — winner: Astria​

In Astria, products, avatars, templates, approvals, and outputs accumulate in a workspace shared by the photographer, the studio, and the agency. In Figma Weave, what accumulates is a library of workflows—valuable, and dependent on the people who authored them.

Choose Figma Weave if...​

  • Your team produces many kinds of visual work, not primarily fashion collections.
  • You want access to many current models with professional editing on one canvas.
  • You have someone who enjoys building and maintaining node-based pipelines.
  • Deep integration with Figma Design is a meaningful advantage for your workflow.

Choose Astria if...​

  • You are producing a fashion collection and want the fashion knowledge supplied, not built.
  • One approved creative direction must carry across catalog, lookbook, campaign, social, and motion.

  • The people who own the creative decision should be able to change it themselves.
  • Review should happen on a shared canvas with voice, alongside your photographer and agency.

The bottom line​

For fashion brands, Astria is the stronger choice: it starts where a node graph would need to be built, and it keeps the creative decision editable by the person who made it. Figma Weave is exceptional general-purpose creative software, and for a design team with broad output it may well be the better investment—just not the faster route to a season's catalog.

What to test before choosing either platform​

Add a second category—jewelry, footwear, beauty—and see what each requires. Have a senior creative review outputs blind for garment fidelity, drape, anatomy, styling, and brand fit. The player is metered separately by impressions with per-thousand overage, and the assistant by its own tokens. The creative question matters more. Brand guidelines are an input Tolstoy consumes per asset; they are not the same as an approved treatment that fixes casting, crop, and styling across a collection. If the brand also wants a shoppable player and an AI assistant on the storefront, those remain available to buy—from Tolstoy or anyone else—without conflating them with production.

A platform serving apparel, skincare, and small appliances optimizes for the common denominator. Fashion's hard parts—drape on a sheer fabric, casting that matches a brand's customer, a crop convention the brand has used for six seasons—are not common-denominator problems. Astria is narrower on purpose, and that is where the depth comes from.

Storefront merchandising and shopper assistance — winner: Tolstoy​

Brands whose bottleneck is on-site merchandising rather than content production should evaluate Tolstoy on that basis—and should ask for the methodology behind the published lift figures.

Where the creative direction lives — winner: Astria​

Feeding brand guidelines into each generation is not the same as approving a treatment once and running it. The first produces assets that are roughly on-brand and individually variable; the second produces a collection that is consistent because consistency is the stored object, not an instruction repeated per asset.

Campaign, editorial, and the rest of the season — winner: Astria​

Tolstoy's content focus is the storefront. A season also needs a lookbook, campaign frames, editorial treatments, and social-native crops, and those are not storefront assets. Astria produces them from the same approved direction, which is both cheaper in effort and more coherent in result.

Collaboration and review — winner: Astria​

Tolstoy's team surface is merchandising and campaign configuration. Astria's is creative review: private brand workspaces, a multiplayer Board with named cursors, and live voice over the actual looks, with external photographers and agencies inside the same workspace.

Collection scale and commercial fit — winner: Astria​

Astria treats the collection as the unit of work and prices to usage—pay for what you create. This article makes no claim that Astria is cheaper; it observes that a bundle discount across three meters is not a production budget. Compounding production value — winner: Astria​

In Astria the workspace accumulates products, avatars, templates, approvals, and outputs, and the next season starts from them. In Tolstoy the durable asset is the merchandising surface on the storefront, which is valuable and does not make the next collection easier to produce.

Choose Tolstoy if...​

  • Your bottleneck is on-site merchandising rather than content production.
  • You want shoppable video, galleries, and an AI shopping assistant from one Shopify-native vendor.
  • Your catalog is mixed-category and general product content is sufficient.
  • Your monthly image and video needs sit comfortably within its token allowances.

Choose Astria if...​

  • You are producing a fashion collection and the imagery is the bottleneck.
  • One approved creative direction must carry across catalog, lookbook, campaign, social, and motion.
  • Category-specific fashion direction matters — apparel, beauty, jewelry, footwear, sports, luxury, editorial.
  • A creative director, photographer, or agency needs to install a workflow other people can reuse.

The bottom line​

For fashion brands, Astria is the stronger choice: it is built for how a collection is produced rather than for how a product page is merchandised. Tolstoy is a capable commerce platform, and its content module is a convenience within that platform rather than a reason to choose it over a production system.

The two are not mutually exclusive. Just do not let a bundle discount decide how your collection gets made.

What to test before choosing either platform​

Check that number against the token allowances of any metered plan before you shortlist. Then run five representative SKUs through both, require PDP, detail, campaign, and social crops, and add a colorway after approval. No. Its published customers span beauty, skincare, and homeware alongside apparel. That breadth is a strength for a general ecommerce team and a limitation for a brand that needs category-specific fashion direction.

Astria. Tolstoy's content module is aimed at product imagery and shoppable video for the storefront. Astria carries one approved direction into lookbook, campaign, editorial, social, and motion.

item.title: Astria vs Browzwear (2026): Which Is Better for Fashion Brands?
item.description: Astria vs Browzwear for fashion brands: 3D design and fit validation versus AI production of catalog, lookbook, and campaign imagery — and where each belongs.
item.content:encoded:
Browzwear and Astria are adjacent, not interchangeable, and any honest comparison has to start there. Browzwear is 30 years of 3D apparel design and development: fabric physics, virtual twins, fit validation, tech packs, fewer physical samples. Astria is a production system for the brand's imagery. The real question buyers ask is narrower and more useful than "which one"—it is whether an existing 3D investment can also produce the catalog and campaign.

The short answer: for producing on-brand imagery across a collection, Astria is the clear winner, and that is the decision this page addresses. For designing and validating garments before manufacture, Browzwear is the right tool and Astria does not compete with it. Plenty of brands should run both.

How we evaluated Astria and Browzwear​

Because these products sit at different points in the calendar, we evaluated them against one shared question: what does it take to get the season's imagery produced? That means looking at inputs required, specialist skills, category and channel coverage, collaboration, collection-scale behavior, and commercial shape — while stating plainly where Browzwear's real value lies, which is upstream.

Quick verdict: Astria vs Browzwear​
